Chapter 8: The Messiness of Healing and the Work of Forgiveness
Healing isn’t a neat, tidy process. If you’ve ever tried to move through pain or loss, you know what I mean—it’s more like a winding, unpredictable journey, full of twists, turns, and unexpected stops.
That’s exactly what the daughter in this story discovers. She’s stumbling through the aftermath of losing her mother, completely unsure of the way forward. Some days, she wakes up feeling strong, ready to take on the world.
But then there are those other days—when even getting out of bed feels impossible.
Regret starts to creep in. She thinks about all the things she never said, the apologies she never made, and those moments of anger that, looking back now, just seem so small.
The guilt? It’s heavy. It presses down on her in ways she never expected. She can’t help but wonder—could she have done more? Should she have been more patient? More understanding? Maybe just… more present?
But these questions don’t have simple answers. And forgiveness—especially forgiving yourself—takes real time.
What she learns, slowly, is that healing isn’t about wiping the slate clean or pretending the past never happened. It’s really about learning to carry those memories, to live with them, and to make peace with her own imperfections.
She starts to realize that both she and her mom did the best they could, with what they knew at the time. Little by little, she forgives herself for the moments she fell short. And she forgives her mother, too—for the times she was tough to love.
Most people don’t realize just how much bravery it takes to walk through grief. The daughter comes to see that healing isn’t a finish line you cross—it’s a practice.
It’s about showing up each day, even when it’s hard. About letting yourself feel the pain, and letting go of what you can’t change. There aren’t any shortcuts here. No quick fixes.
It’s just the steady, quiet work of putting one foot in front of the other.
And over time, she starts to find moments of peace. She learns to celebrate the good memories, to honor the tough ones, and to accept that both are part of her story.
The process isn’t over—and maybe it never will be. But she begins to trust herself, knowing that, step by step, she’ll find her way.
